<section id="overview" class="content-section">

The Counter Roll is a high-risk, high-reward escape technique executed when caught in D'arce Control from the bottom position. Rather than fighting the choke directly or attempting to extract the trapped arm, this technique uses the opponent's committed choking pressure against them by rolling through their position. The defender initiates a rolling motion toward the choking arm, using the opponent's own forward pressure and grip commitment as momentum to complete the reversal.

This technique exemplifies the principle that sometimes the best defense is to move with the attack rather than against it. When an opponent commits heavily to finishing the D'arce choke, they often sacrifice positional stability. The Counter Roll exploits this vulnerability by timing the roll precisely when the opponent drives their weight forward. The rolling motion carries the opponent over and lands the defender in top position, typically side control or a scramble situation.

The Counter Roll requires precise timing, understanding of weight distribution, and the courage to commit fully to the movement despite being in a compromised choking position. It is most effective when executed before the choke is fully locked, during the transition phase when the opponent is adjusting their grip or position. Advanced practitioners use this technique as a calculated risk when other escapes have failed or when they recognize the opponent's positional commitment creates an opening.

**From Position**: [[D'arce Control/Bottom]]
**Success Rates**: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%

</section>

<section id="possible-outcomes" class="content-section">

## Possible Outcomes

| Result | Position | Probability |
|--------|----------|-------------|
| Success | [[Side Control]] | 50% |
| Success | [[Scramble Position]] | 15% |
| Failure | [[D'arce Control]] | 25% |
| Counter | [[Mount]] | 10% |


</section>



<section id="key-principles" class="content-section">

## Key Principles
- Time the roll during opponent's forward pressure or grip adjustment rather than when they are settled and stable
- Commit fully to the rolling motion once initiated as partial attempts leave you in worse position
- Use your free arm to post and guide the roll direction while maintaining some neck protection
- Roll toward the choking arm side not away from it to use their weight and grip commitment as momentum
- Keep your chin tucked throughout the roll to maintain choke defense until the position reverses
- Accelerate through the middle of the roll where you are most vulnerable to maximize momentum


</section>

<section id="setup-requirements" class="content-section">

## Prerequisites
- Caught in D'arce Control with opponent's arm threaded under your armpit and around your neck
- Opponent is driving forward with their weight committed to finishing the choke
- Your free arm is available to post and initiate the rolling motion
- The choke is not yet fully locked allowing some movement and neck protection
- You have identified the direction of opponent's weight distribution and pressure


</section>

<section id="execution-steps" class="content-section">

## Execution Steps
1. **Assess choke depth**: Evaluate how deep the D'arce grip is locked. This technique works best when the choke is not yet fully tight and you still have ability to tuck your chin and move your body. (Timing: Immediately upon recognizing the D'arce grip)
2. **Position free arm**: Place your free hand (the arm not trapped in the choke) on the mat beside your hip on the side you will roll toward. This arm will post and guide the rolling direction. (Timing: As opponent adjusts grip or drives forward)
3. **Load hips**: Shift your hips toward the direction of the roll by bridging slightly and angling your pelvis. This creates the rotational momentum needed to carry your body and your opponent over. (Timing: When opponent commits weight forward)
4. **Initiate roll**: Push off your posting arm while simultaneously driving your hips over in the rolling direction. Turn your head into the roll and use your entire body to generate rotational force. (Timing: At peak of opponent's forward pressure)
5. **Accelerate through**: Commit fully to the roll by continuing the rotation even as you feel resistance. Pull your trapped arm tight to your body and keep chin tucked as you pass through the vulnerable mid-roll position. (Timing: Continuously through the rotation)
6. **Establish top position**: As the roll completes, immediately work to establish side control or mount by driving your weight into opponent's chest and securing an underhook or crossface before they can re-establish the choke grip. (Timing: Immediately upon completing rotation)


</section>

<section id="common-counters" class="content-section">

## Opponent Counters
- **Opponent sprawls and drives hips away to prevent the roll from completing** (Effectiveness: High) - Your Response: If they sprawl early, abort the roll attempt and return to standard arm extraction escapes. Their sprawl releases forward pressure needed to finish the choke.
- **Opponent switches to anaconda grip configuration during your roll attempt** (Effectiveness: Medium) - Your Response: Continue the roll if already committed as the anaconda switch often loosens the original grip. The position change during switching creates escape opportunities.
- **Opponent posts their free hand to block the roll direction** (Effectiveness: Medium) - Your Response: If they post, their grip strength on the choke typically decreases. Use this moment to extract your trapped arm and transition to turtle or guard recovery.
- **Opponent tightens the choke and sits back rather than driving forward** (Effectiveness: High) - Your Response: Abort the counter roll and switch to arm extraction or granby roll escape. The counter roll requires their forward commitment to work effectively.


</section>

<section id="common-mistakes" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## Common Mistakes
- **Mistake**: Attempting the roll when the choke is already fully locked and tight
  - **Consequence**: The roll fails to reverse position and you lose consciousness during the attempt due to the accelerated blood choke effect
  - **Correction**: Only attempt counter roll when choke is in setup phase with some space remaining. If fully locked, prioritize tap or immediate arm extraction.
- **Mistake**: Rolling away from the choke rather than into it
  - **Consequence**: Creates space that allows opponent to tighten the choke further and follow your movement to maintain dominant position
  - **Correction**: Always roll toward the choking arm side. This direction uses their grip commitment as momentum and keeps you moving into them.
- **Mistake**: Half-committing to the roll and stopping mid-rotation
  - **Consequence**: Getting stuck on your back in an even worse position with the choke potentially tighter and no positional improvement
  - **Correction**: Once you initiate the roll, commit fully and accelerate through. Partial attempts are worse than not attempting at all.
- **Mistake**: Forgetting to post with free arm and relying only on hip movement
  - **Consequence**: Insufficient rotational force to complete the roll, especially against heavier opponents
  - **Correction**: The posting arm is essential for generating and directing rotational force. Plant it firmly before initiating and push hard through the roll.
- **Mistake**: Lifting chin and extending neck during the roll
  - **Consequence**: Allows opponent's choking arm to sink deeper under your jaw during the rotation, potentially finishing the choke mid-roll
  - **Correction**: Maintain strict chin tuck throughout the entire roll. Your chin should never leave your chest until you have completed the reversal and established top position.


</section>

<section id="training-progressions" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## Training Progressions
**Week 1-2** - Rolling mechanics
Practice the rolling motion without any choke threat. Partner holds light head and arm control while you drill the posting arm position, hip loading, and roll direction. Focus on smooth, complete rotations ending in top position.
(Resistance: None)

**Week 3-4** - Timing recognition
Partner applies D'arce grip at 30% pressure. Practice identifying the optimal timing window when they drive forward. Drill reading their weight shift and initiating the roll at the right moment. Partner provides feedback on timing.
(Resistance: Light)

**Week 5-6** - Pressure adaptation
Partner increases D'arce pressure to 60%. Work on maintaining composure while identifying timing windows. Practice aborting when timing is wrong and switching to alternative escapes. Develop decision-making under realistic pressure.
(Resistance: Medium)

**Week 7+** - Live application
Incorporate counter roll into positional sparring from D'arce Control scenarios. Partner attacks at full resistance while you choose between counter roll, arm extraction, or other escapes based on their pressure and grip depth. Refine success rate through repetition.
(Resistance: Full)



</section>

<section id="variants-and-adaptations" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## Variations
**Sit-out Counter Roll**: Instead of rolling directly over, combine the counter roll with a sit-out motion by swinging your hips away as you initiate the turn. This creates a hybrid movement that can transition to turtle or single leg if the full roll fails. (When to use: When opponent is not fully committed forward and you need an escape option that does not require their pressure to complete)

**Leg Hook Counter Roll**: As you initiate the roll, hook your inside leg behind opponent's near leg to anchor their lower body. This prevents them from stepping around or adjusting their base, increasing the success rate of the reversal. (When to use: When opponent has a wide base that might allow them to post and prevent the roll)

**Back Take Counter Roll**: Rather than completing the roll to side control, use the rotational momentum to spin behind opponent and establish back control with a seatbelt grip as they fall forward. (When to use: When opponent is very committed forward with poor base and you recognize the back take opportunity during the roll)



</section>

<section id="knowledge-assessment" class="content-section">

## Test Your Knowledge
**Q1**: What is the primary goal of Counter Roll?
**A**: The primary goal is to reverse the position when caught in D'arce Control by rolling through your opponent's committed pressure, ending in top position such as side control. It uses their weight and grip commitment against them rather than fighting the choke directly.

**Q2**: What position do you start Counter Roll from?
**A**: Counter Roll is executed from D'arce Control Bottom, when your opponent has threaded their arm under your armpit and around your neck in the D'arce choke configuration. You are typically on your side or in turtle with the choking arm locked.

**Q3**: Why must you roll toward the choking arm rather than away from it?
**A**: Rolling toward the choking arm uses your opponent's grip commitment and forward pressure as momentum for the reversal. Rolling away creates space that allows them to tighten the choke and follow your movement. The direction into the choke keeps you moving against their base while their grip actually assists the rotation.

**Q4**: Your opponent sits back and tightens the choke instead of driving forward - should you attempt the counter roll?
**A**: No, abort the counter roll attempt. This technique requires opponent's forward weight commitment to generate the momentum needed for reversal. When they sit back, switch to arm extraction, granby roll, or other escapes that do not depend on their forward pressure. Attempting counter roll against a seated opponent results in failed rotation with a tighter choke.

**Q5**: What is the function of your free arm in the Counter Roll?
**A**: The free arm posts on the mat to generate and direct rotational force. It acts as a pivot point and push-off surface that initiates the rolling motion. Without the posting arm, you rely only on hip movement which is insufficient to complete the roll, especially against heavier opponents. Plant it firmly beside your hip on the side you will roll toward.

**Q6**: How do you manage the choke threat during the roll itself?
**A**: Maintain strict chin tuck throughout the entire rotation to prevent the choking arm from sinking deeper under your jaw. Pull your trapped arm tight to your body during the roll. The mid-roll position is most vulnerable, so accelerate through this phase rather than hesitating. The roll should be fast enough that the choke does not have time to fully lock during the transition.

**Q7**: What timing cue indicates the optimal moment to initiate the counter roll?
**A**: The optimal moment is when your opponent drives their weight forward aggressively, commits to tightening the choke by adjusting their grip, or walks their hips around to improve their finishing angle. These movements shift their balance and base forward, creating the unstable platform needed for the reversal. Initiating during their adjustment phase catches them mid-transition.

**Q8**: What should you do immediately after completing the roll?
**A**: Immediately establish top position control before opponent can re-establish the choke grip. Drive your weight into their chest, secure an underhook or crossface, and work to consolidate side control or advance to mount. Do not pause after the roll completes - the transition is not finished until you have secured dominant position and eliminated the submission threat.

**Q9**: When should you abort a counter roll attempt and what alternatives should you use?
**A**: Abort when: the choke is fully locked with no space remaining, opponent sits back instead of driving forward, or opponent sprawls and removes their weight commitment. Alternatives include arm extraction to eliminate the arm-in configuration, granby roll to recover guard, back door escape to turtle, or simply tapping if the choke is past the point of safe escape.

**Q10**: How does the leg hook variant improve counter roll success rate?
**A**: Hooking your inside leg behind opponent's near leg anchors their lower body and prevents them from stepping around to maintain base or posting to block the roll direction. This removes their primary defensive option against the reversal. Use this variant when opponent has a wide base that would otherwise allow them to adjust and stop your rotation.



</section>

<section id="safety-considerations" class="content-section">

## Safety Considerations

Counter Roll carries significant risk because it is performed while already caught in a choke. Never attempt this technique when the D'arce is fully locked with no space remaining between your neck and opponent's arm. Tap immediately if you feel lightheadedness, vision changes, or loss of strength during the attempt. In training, communicate with your partner about the pressure level and have them release if you tap during the roll. Avoid training this technique when fatigued as compromised judgment increases the risk of waiting too long to tap. Beginners should drill the mechanics extensively with zero resistance before adding any choke pressure. The technique should be considered a calculated risk option, not a primary escape.

</section>

<section id="position-integration" class="content-section">

## Position Integration

Counter Roll fits into the D'arce defense system as a high-risk option when standard escapes have failed or are unavailable. It integrates with other front headlock defenses and represents the aggressive end of the escape spectrum. The technique connects D'arce Control Bottom to various top positions including Side Control, Mount, and scramble scenarios. Practitioners should develop this alongside arm extraction, granby roll, and back door escape to have a complete defensive toolbox. Counter Roll is most valuable in competition contexts where the alternative is losing by submission, making the risk-reward calculation favorable. It chains naturally into top position attacks once the reversal is complete.

</section>
